chapter_theme: The sarukkam turns from the kings of the plain to the Vidyadhara ridge: a hill of gods, groves and lovers, then its golden city Ratanupura-Chakravalam and its king, who has every virtue and learning but lacks grace toward the lowly.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge

119.reading: The poet leaves the kings' talk where it stands and promises to tell of the Vidyadhara country on the ridge.
119.event: The poet turns from the kings of the plain to the city of the Vidyadharas.

120.reading: The Vidyadhara hill, pale as moonlit ground, stretches to the sea and rises so high that the jewelled mansions of the sky stand aside for it.
120.nuance: Lines 3-4 are hard to construe; the sense of the hill outreaching the sky's mansions is the likely one.

121.reading: Gods gather with their women to play in the groves, and the sparks that fall from their jewels make the groves look like the red evening sky.

122.reading: Heavenly women and their loving mates drink the coral-lipped nectar and embrace, so crushed garlands scent the wishing-tree groves.

123.reading: Kinnara gods dwell with their women in the sandal groves, which are full of a cool divine fragrance.

124.reading: A cool wind stirs the mandara grove and the tulasi, and pollen and flower-honey spill over the breasts of the heavenly women like water.
124.nuance: The verb in line 4 can also mean the scent leaps upon them; the image of pollen and honey as bath-water is the likelier.

125.reading: In the sandal bowers beds of leaves are set; those who still bear flesh delight in pleasure there, while those of the sky stay day after day.
125.nuance: The contrast between the fleshly and the sky-dwellers in lines 3-4 depends on a rare compound and may be read as two groups of lovers or as men against gods.

126.reading: Women of fine hair play with the hill's youths, and the scented powder of their play falls and stains the sleeping rocks.
126.nuance: The edition's word division in lines 3-4 is doubtful.

127.reading: The red dye of women's feet, learning a walk of their own, marks the rocks and draws the eyes of their lovers.
127.nuance: Lines 1-2 are uncertain in wording; the footprint-dye is certain from line 3.

128.reading: Streams run down golden rocks where naga maidens bathe, mixing with the rut of the elephants and smelling of jasmine.

129.reading: The flowers are golden lotuses and the groves are wishing-tree gardens, so the poet asks what more need be told of the Vidyadhara ridge.
129.nuance: The question of line 4 is a figure of speech that cuts the description short; its exact force is not settled.

130.reading: On the southern ridge of the Vidyadharas, where the moon rests on the hill, a golden city called Ratanupura-Chakravalam is said to stand.
130.nuance: The city's name is given here for the first time; the title of the sarukkam comes from it.

131.reading: Gold plantains ripen red-gold, and their gleam seems to drip as juice on the garland-wearing women's pearl-lipped talk.
131.nuance: The wording of lines 1-2 is corrupt or very compressed; only the gold fruit and its glow are firm.

132.reading: Heaps of areca nut under the moonlit silver spathes look like fallen gems and ripe gold clusters.
132.nuance: The sense of line 1 turns on a doubtful word; the image of the nuts as fallen jewels is clear.

133.reading: The wishing-trees' radiance and scattered parijata flowers look like scattered fire, and the golden mansions' doors shine behind the trees.

134.reading: Lovers sport together, ruining their sandal paste and sweating, and a wind scented with the groves and bees makes the flowers sway.

135.reading: Mango, ashoka and sandal sprouts in flower let their honey drop, and the swaying devadaru drops it too as the wind bears the scent.

136.reading: The divine river, groves and flowering bowers of this place are such pleasant haunts that all the noise they make is the love-god's own tumult.
136.nuance: The place is made an arena of Kama's play, so the setting prepares the later court scenes of desire among the Vidyadharas.

137.reading: The king of that city, lord of war-elephant kings, is faultless and named by a riddle of fire and syllables that the poet leaves to the reader; who could describe him?
137.nuance: The name is given as a puzzle in lines 2-3 and cannot be fixed with certainty from the verse alone.

138.reading: His white umbrella's shade reaches the world's end, fierce-eyed elephant kings bow to him, and he shines in victory with a saffron-smeared, garlanded chest.
138.event: The Vidyadhara king receives the homage of rival elephant kings.

139.reading: He has mastered every branch of knowledge, the Vidyadharas fear him, his wishes are met, and he lets no false word pass but keeps to truth.
139.nuance: The word வெச்சனும் in line 4 is obscure; the claim of truthfulness rests on மெய்ம்மை.

claims.claim: a king should keep to truth and let no falsehood pass his lips

140.reading: In the days when this Vidyadhara king guards the world under his one sceptre, there is a single fault among his virtues: he lacks grace toward the lowly lives beneath him.
140.nuance: The poet praises the king's virtues in the previous verses and then names one flaw; compassion toward lower creatures is the Jain test of a ruler's goodness, though the verse itself names no school.

claims.claim: a ruler with every virtue is still at fault if he lacks grace toward the lowest living beings

141.reading: While the golden-crowned spear-bearing Vidyadhara king rules the realm, the plantain-like banners tremble.
141.nuance: Whether the trembling banners are an omen of the fault just named or simply a sign of his might is not clear in the Tamil.

142.reading: In the days when his bright old crown shines, the brows of the women press on the men like bent bows.
142.nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe; the closing bow-like brow image is firm.

links.note: Verse 140 faults a mighty king for want of grace to the lowly; Kural 557 says that a king's lack of tender regard is to his people as lack of rain to the earth.
links.teaches: The epic names one flaw in a king otherwise perfect, so the Kural's claim that lack of regard undoes all else is tested against a ruler praised for everything else.

gains.a: A measure of the flaw's weight, which the verse names without saying how much it costs.
gains.b: A concrete king whose every other virtue stands, so the couplet's rule faces a hard case.

links.note: Kural 549 counts guarding the people and removing wrongdoing as the king's work and no fault; verse 140 faults a king on the ground of grace toward the lowest lives, which the Kural's list does not ask of him.
links.teaches: The epic widens the king's duty to grace toward all lowly lives, where the Kural's duty stops at the people and the removal of wrongdoers, so the two hold different measures of a good ruler.

gains.a: A rival standard, the Kural's, by which the king is judged only on what he does to his people.
gains.b: A test of its limit: a king who punishes wrongdoers by the Kural's rule may still lack grace toward lower creatures.

links.note: Both Jain epics describe a Vidyadhara city by its splendour, this one as a golden city on the southern ridge, the other as a casket of gems opened.
links.teaches: Both epics fix the Vidyadhara realm in the reader's mind as a city of gems and gold above the plain, so the genre's convention is clear from the pair.

source_issues: Verses 120, 124-127, 131-133, 135, 137, 139, 141-142: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's word division and compressed grammar; flagged uncertain.
Verse 137 line 3: the name-riddle is left unresolved.
